This is a fictional physics training scenario, not a real accident. An aircraft descends from thirty thousand feet to eighteen thousand feet over forty seconds, then levels off. Altitude means height above a reference level. The descent rate is the change in altitude divided by elapsed time. An animation can show the aircraft moving down along an altitude curve while a numerical readout follows its height. A submarine descends through seawater toward a depth of one thousand meters at one meter per second. Hydrostatic pressure, the squeezing force of water per unit area, increases with depth because more water lies overhead. The simple model uses pressure equals water density multiplied by gravitational acceleration and depth. This model is an illustration, not an engineering prediction of structural failure. Meanwhile, a ship moves through the Strait of Hormuz along an explicitly synthetic route. Its coordinates are invented for a demonstration and must not be presented as live AIS observations. Radar sweeps rotate through changing angles to illustrate how a scanning direction moves. Radar uses radio waves and echoes to detect objects. The flight, submarine, ship, and radar examples should each show their own kind of motion. Do not treat a weather forecast as a radar measurement, and do not treat an illustrative ship path as an observed track.
